title: Apply layout principles for conservation and infrastructure

lessons.title: Reading the land and planning the layout
lessons.html:
Why layout matters

The way fields, camps, roads, fences, buildings and water points are placed on a farm affects erosion, water use, the cost of daily work and the safety of people and animals. A good layout works with the land. A poor layout causes gullies along roads, waterlogged lands, animals walking far to water, and wasted time and fuel.

Reading the land

Before planning, walk the farm and look at:

  • Slope – steep, gentle or flat. Steep land is at more risk of erosion.
  • Contours – lines joining points of the same height. Water flows at right angles to contours, downhill.
  • Natural drainage lines – where water flows after rain, including vleis and streams.
  • Soil types – deep and well-drained, shallow, stony, wet.
  • Existing veld and trees, wetlands and sensitive areas.
  • Access – roads, gates, neighbours, power lines.

A farm map or aerial photo helps. Mark these features on it.

Land use planning

Match each area to its best use:

  • Deep soils on gentle slopes – cultivated lands.
  • Steep or shallow soils – grazing, woodlots or natural veld.
  • Wetlands and river banks – protected; no ploughing.
  • Flat, well-drained, high ground – buildings, kraals and stores.

Marking contours

Contours can be found with a simple A-frame level or a line level, or with a dumpy level or GPS by a trained person. Peg points of equal height across the slope and join them. These lines guide contour banks, planting rows and swales. Your supervisor will show you the method the farm uses.

Safety

Watch for holes, snakes and steep drops when walking the land. Call before any digging near power lines or buried pipes.

lessons.title: Laying out conservation works and infrastructure
lessons.html:
Conservation structures

  • Contour banks – low earth banks built along the contour on cultivated land, with a slight fall so excess water flows slowly to a safe outlet.
  • Grassed waterways – wide, shallow channels kept under grass that carry water from contour banks safely downhill. Never plough them.
  • Diversion banks – stop water from higher ground running onto lands, roads or buildings.
  • Strip cropping and buffer strips – strips of grass or other cover between crop strips or along streams.
  • Gully control – stone packs, brush packs and grass planting to slow water and trap soil.

The Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 requires land users to protect cultivated land against erosion and to protect wetlands and watercourses.

Roads and tracks

  • Plan roads along the contour or at a gentle slope where possible, not straight down steep slopes.
  • Build mitre drains or humps to turn water off the road at regular intervals.
  • Cross streams at stable points with proper drifts or culverts.
  • Keep roads on firm, well-drained ground.

Fences and camps

  • Lay out camps so each has water and so similar veld types are in the same camp, allowing even grazing.
  • Place gates in corners near water and where animals naturally move, not in drainage lines.
  • Avoid fences running straight down steep slopes; animal paths along them become gullies.

Water points

  • Place troughs so animals do not walk too far, and on firm, well-drained ground.
  • Move or protect troughs where the area around them becomes trampled and bare.
  • Keep dams, troughs and pipelines away from sources of pollution.

Buildings and kraals

  • Build on high, well-drained ground, away from flood lines and streams.
  • Keep chemical stores, fuel and manure heaps away from water sources and houses.
  • Plan easy access for trucks and safe handling of animals.

Key points

  • Read slope, contours, drainage, soils and sensitive areas before planning.
  • Match each area to its best use; protect wetlands and river banks.
  • Use contour banks, grassed waterways and diversion banks to control runoff.
  • Lay roads on gentle gradients with drains to turn water off.
  • Place camps, gates, troughs and buildings to suit the land and reduce erosion.
